_causes.empty_authoritative: no visible workload, so no binding to resolve
_causes.partial: two bound workloads on two roles; the decision authority names one role as a gap, so it renders withheld beside a decided role
_causes.partial_no_account_policy_context: no organizations:account-policy-context row in the generation, so the identity graph reports ACCOUNT_POLICY_CONTEXT_ABSENT -- NOT a standalone account
_causes.partial_unresolved_role_id: binding whose canonical role has no AWS RoleId
_causes.ready: one ACTIVE binding, decision generation present, one decision row
_causes.standalone_account: an account-policy-context row with organization_present=false: a positively standalone account, no org edges, no control policies

_provenance: Each payload is the literal return value of scripts.estate_identity_access.build_estate_identity_access, run over a real-shape in-memory graph. Decision rows are real RoleActionDecision instances and decision gaps are real RoleActionDecisionGap instances, validated by the real contracts. Every status difference comes from a difference in the INPUT rows; no output was edited to reach a state. read_active_projection, verify_generation and fetch_role_decisions are substituted for the run at the same seam the projection suite uses, because they would otherwise need a live Neptune generation -- see the module docstring for exactly what that does and does not cover. Serialisation is the pinned runtime's: pydantic 2.12.5 renders a (str, Enum) member as its value and a UTC datetime as RFC 3339 with a Z suffix. That is asserted on a real record before rendering and walked over the finished payload; json.dumps carries no default= fallback, so nothing is stringified in.

relationship_capabilities.detail: Whether this account belongs to an AWS Organization, and which one. `organization_present` is an explicit boolean the normalizer refuses to default, so a standalone account is a positive claim and an ABSENT row is neither claim -- the payload says ACCOUNT_POLICY_CONTEXT_ABSENT rather than reporting an account that answers to nobody. There is no organizations:organization resource type, so the far end is an organization ID.

The complete account-to-root placement chain, emitted one child->parent hop at a time with a `depth` (1 is the account's own parent). The normalizer refuses a hierarchy that does not start at this account and end at a ROOT, so a partial chain is never published. OUs and roots are not projected resources, so each endpoint is an OU identifier.

Resource control policies, kept as their own family rather than folded into the SCP one. An SCP bounds what principals IN this account may do; an RCP bounds what anyone may do TO this account's resources. They are separate AWS control types with separate enablement status, and a screen that merged them would answer a question about principals with a policy that governs resources.

Service control policies attached at EVERY layer of the hierarchy, not only directly to the account: an SCP on the root bounds this account exactly as one attached to it does, and each edge carries `inherited` and `attached_at_target_type` so the two are distinguishable without being separable. When the SERVICE_CONTROL_POLICY type is DISABLED org-wide the account node says so in `control_policy_type_statuses`, which is why there are no attachments -- a reason, not an empty list. Policy DOCUMENTS are not carried on this bounded map; `document_present` says one exists.

cyntro_data.projection.neptune_graph.observations.RoleAssumptionProjector is generation-bound and declares plane OBSERVED, but nothing in the tree calls it -- only two re-export lines reference it. No edge of this type is ever written.

Written only by non-generation-bound writers. It is also classified two incompatible ways by installed registries: TOPOLOGY_INVENTORY in unified/evidence/contract.py and Plane.OBSERVED in unified/quality/edge_registry.py. The canonical observed producer that would settle it is the unwired one above.

Written only by non-generation-bound writers, one of them behind a feature flag. Role chaining is commonly source-role to target-role, so a target-anchored view would additionally need incoming traversal, which this contract does not offer.
Written only by non-generation-bound writers. Not interchangeable with ASSUMES_ROLE or ASSUMES_ROLE_ACTUAL: different producers, different planes, different directions.

The active canonical path is not an edge: it is the versioned BehavioralSummary DATA_ACCESS grain, and its one bounded read (cyntro_data.projection.behavioral_reader.data_access_by_asset_cypher) is ASSET-anchored -- it UNWINDs a caller-supplied $asset_uids list and matches data_asset_uid, with no principal predicate. principal_uid appears only on the way out. Producing role-anchored output would require enumerating the tenant's whole data-asset universe first and filtering after the fact, which is the unbounded scan this contract forbids, and the 2000-row cap would truncate it silently. A principal-anchored bounded read must be added beside it before this family can be served here; it must not be inverted in the consumer.
Written only by legacy collectors and demo seeding, none of them generation-bound. Configured grants for a role are served here from the decision authority instead, which is hash-verified.
Account/OU placement, not role authority, and its only writer is not generation-bound. The membership FACT is served as ACCOUNT_IN_ORGANIZATION above; this edge type remains undrawable.
Account/OU placement, not role authority, and its only writer is not generation-bound. The placement chain is served as ACCOUNT_IN_ORG_UNIT above; this edge type remains undrawable.

Organisation-level control attachment. Reaching it needs a bounded account/org path, not a role edge, and its only writer (collectors/organizations_collector.py) carries no generation at all. The EDGE stays unreadable; the FACT is served as ACCOUNT_LIMITED_BY_SCP and ACCOUNT_LIMITED_BY_RCP above, from the canonical organizations:account-policy-context resource.
Written only by the Identity Center collector, which is not generation-bound. Distinct from MEMBER_OF_CLUSTER, an RDS topology edge; the two must not be coalesced.

Inline policy documents live on the principal and have no independent identity in AWS, so there is no resource to point at. The grant is reported with its policy name and document; the reason code says the far endpoint is not a node, so a consumer does not go looking for one.

Attached managed policy ARNs, carried on iam:role and iam:user and projected as canonical JSON. An ARN that also exists as an iam:policy resource in the same generation resolves to that node; an AWS-managed ARN usually does not, and is reported as an unresolved endpoint rather than dropped.
The boundary ARN on iam:role and iam:user. A boundary caps what the attachments above can grant, so a consumer that draws grants without it overstates every principal that has one.

The *-authorization sibling resource family -- s3:bucket-authorization, function-authorization, key-authorization, queue-authorization, topic-authorization, secret-authorization, event-bus-authorization, vpc-endpoint-authorization. Each is a canonical resource in its own right with a DISTINCT resource_uid from the thing it protects, bridged to the same legacy node, so the grant is generation-owned like any other inventory fact. This is the resource-policy side of access; the identity side is the three grant families above.
Accepted only after decision_fetch.verify_generation proves the pinned generation's exact count and set hash, and the conserved role-level open-universe gaps are checked by count and hash.

The role's own assume-role policy document: who MAY assume it, which is configured state and is exactly what CAN_ASSUME and TRUSTS below could not supply. It is not evidence that anyone DID assume the role -- that is ASSUMED_ROLE_OBSERVED, still unavailable -- and the two must not be merged on a screen.
A workload/resource dependency edge written by event and scheduler collectors, not a role authority edge.
Not a role-outgoing edge at all: it runs from an external principal to a resource-policy grant. Anchoring it on a role returns nothing regardless of generation.

The iam:user-credential-state sibling fact: access keys with status and last-used service/region, console access and MFA. Configured and observed at once, and the record says which is which. Every field is paired with an acquisition flag (access_keys_acquired, console_access_acquired, mfa_acquired) because a role without iam:ListAccessKeys produces absence, not zero; SOURCE_CALL_NOT_ACQUIRED is carried per record when a flag is false rather than reporting a user with no credentials.

Group membership from iam:user.group_names. Distinct from the MEMBER_OF entry below, which is the Identity Center collector's non-generation-bound edge: this one is canonical and generation-owned. There is no iam:group resource type, so the far end is a group NAME. Groups carry policy attachments of their own that this contract therefore cannot resolve, and the reason code is what tells a consumer not to present membership as a complete permission path.
A resource dependency edge, not a role authority edge.

They are separate AWS control types with separate enablement status, and a screen that merged them would answer a question about principals with a policy that governs resources.

Service control policies attached at EVERY layer of the hierarchy, not only directly to the account: an SCP on the root bounds this account exactly as one attached to it does, and each edge carries `inherited` and `attached_at_target_type` so the two are distinguishable without being separable. When the SERVICE_CONTROL_POLICY type is DISABLED org-wide the account node says so in `control_policy_type_statuses`, which is why there are no attachments -- a reason, not an empty list. Policy DOCUMENTS are not carried on this bounded map; `document_present` says one exists.

cyntro_data.projection.neptune_graph.observations.RoleAssumptionProjector is generation-bound and declares plane OBSERVED, but nothing in the tree calls it -- only two re-export lines reference it. No edge of this type is ever written.

Written only by non-generation-bound writers. It is also classified two incompatible ways by installed registries: TOPOLOGY_INVENTORY in unified/evidence/contract.py and Plane.OBSERVED in unified/quality/edge_registry.py. The canonical observed producer that would settle it is the unwired one above.

Written only by non-generation-bound writers, one of them behind a feature flag. Role chaining is commonly source-role to target-role, so a target-anchored view would additionally need incoming traversal, which this contract does not offer.
Written only by non-generation-bound writers. Not interchangeable with ASSUMES_ROLE or ASSUMES_ROLE_ACTUAL: different producers, different planes, different directions.

The active canonical path is not an edge: it is the versioned BehavioralSummary DATA_ACCESS grain, and its one bounded read (cyntro_data.projection.behavioral_reader.data_access_by_asset_cypher) is ASSET-anchored -- it UNWINDs a caller-supplied $asset_uids list and matches data_asset_uid, with no principal predicate. principal_uid appears only on the way out. Producing role-anchored output would require enumerating the tenant's whole data-asset universe first and filtering after the fact, which is the unbounded scan this contract forbids, and the 2000-row cap would truncate it silently. A principal-anchored bounded read must be added beside it before this family can be served here; it must not be inverted in the consumer.
Written only by legacy collectors and demo seeding, none of them generation-bound. Configured grants for a role are served here from the decision authority instead, which is hash-verified.
Account/OU placement, not role authority, and its only writer is not generation-bound. The membership FACT is served as ACCOUNT_IN_ORGANIZATION above; this edge type remains undrawable.
Account/OU placement, not role authority, and its only writer is not generation-bound. The placement chain is served as ACCOUNT_IN_ORG_UNIT above; this edge type remains undrawable.

Organisation-level control attachment. Reaching it needs a bounded account/org path, not a role edge, and its only writer (collectors/organizations_collector.py) carries no generation at all. The EDGE stays unreadable; the FACT is served as ACCOUNT_LIMITED_BY_SCP and ACCOUNT_LIMITED_BY_RCP above, from the canonical organizations:account-policy-context resource.
Written only by the Identity Center collector, which is not generation-bound. Distinct from MEMBER_OF_CLUSTER, an RDS topology edge; the two must not be coalesced.

Inline policy documents live on the principal and have no independent identity in AWS, so there is no resource to point at. The grant is reported with its policy name and document; the reason code says the far endpoint is not a node, so a consumer does not go looking for one.

Attached managed policy ARNs, carried on iam:role and iam:user and projected as canonical JSON. An ARN that also exists as an iam:policy resource in the same generation resolves to that node; an AWS-managed ARN usually does not, and is reported as an unresolved endpoint rather than dropped.
The boundary ARN on iam:role and iam:user. A boundary caps what the attachments above can grant, so a consumer that draws grants without it overstates every principal that has one.

The *-authorization sibling resource family -- s3:bucket-authorization, function-authorization, key-authorization, queue-authorization, topic-authorization, secret-authorization, event-bus-authorization, vpc-endpoint-authorization. Each is a canonical resource in its own right with a DISTINCT resource_uid from the thing it protects, bridged to the same legacy node, so the grant is generation-owned like any other inventory fact. This is the resource-policy side of access; the identity side is the three grant families above.
Accepted only after decision_fetch.verify_generation proves the pinned generation's exact count and set hash, and the conserved role-level open-universe gaps are checked by count and hash.

The role's own assume-role policy document: who MAY assume it, which is configured state and is exactly what CAN_ASSUME and TRUSTS below could not supply. It is not evidence that anyone DID assume the role -- that is ASSUMED_ROLE_OBSERVED, still unavailable -- and the two must not be merged on a screen.
A workload/resource dependency edge written by event and scheduler collectors, not a role authority edge.
Not a role-outgoing edge at all: it runs from an external principal to a resource-policy grant. Anchoring it on a role returns nothing regardless of generation.

The iam:user-credential-state sibling fact: access keys with status and last-used service/region, console access and MFA. Configured and observed at once, and the record says which is which. Every field is paired with an acquisition flag (access_keys_acquired, console_access_acquired, mfa_acquired) because a role without iam:ListAccessKeys produces absence, not zero; SOURCE_CALL_NOT_ACQUIRED is carried per record when a flag is false rather than reporting a user with no credentials.

Group membership from iam:user.group_names. Distinct from the MEMBER_OF entry below, which is the Identity Center collector's non-generation-bound edge: this one is canonical and generation-owned. There is no iam:group resource type, so the far end is a group NAME. Groups carry policy attachments of their own that this contract therefore cannot resolve, and the reason code is what tells a consumer not to present membership as a complete permission path.
A resource dependency edge, not a role authority edge.

Generation-owned canonical binding. The active pointer must declare COMPLETE workload binding coverage with an exact count, an exact set hash and a validated projection receipt before this projection is built at all.

Whether this account belongs to an AWS Organization, and which one. `organization_present` is an explicit boolean the normalizer refuses to default, so a standalone account is a positive claim and an ABSENT row is neither claim -- the payload says ACCOUNT_POLICY_CONTEXT_ABSENT rather than reporting an account that answers to nobody. There is no organizations:organization resource type, so the far end is an organization ID.

The complete account-to-root placement chain, emitted one child->parent hop at a time with a `depth` (1 is the account's own parent). The normalizer refuses a hierarchy that does not start at this account and end at a ROOT, so a partial chain is never published. OUs and roots are not projected resources, so each endpoint is an OU identifier.
